description: My name is Vaibhav Asvin, and I am very interested in space. At the moment, I am a pretty decent mathematician and coder. We have already built our team, and we are no longer looking for another new member. Our other member is named Sachin Shankar, and he is an avid astronomer, and has a lot of knowledge about space. He too, is quite astonished at the prospect of the space outside of the Earth.
summary:
Forman is a website where you build a spacecraft or Moon/Mars habitat module in 3D and see how a fire inside it would behave. You place walls, fabrics, wiring and storage, pick materials like cotton, Nomex or Kapton, and choose orbit, the Moon or Mars. Forman marks each area safe, marginal or hazardous, and its super intelligence (SI) suggests safer materials or layouts, with the tradeoffs in weight and cost. You can also start from a photo, sketch or 3D model of a real space and compare designs.

Flames behave differently in low gravity. On Earth, hot air rises and pulls fresh oxygen into a fire. In microgravity that flow mostly stops, so flames turn round, burn slower and can survive where they’d go out on Earth. NASA has run more than 1,100 microgravity fire tests, but very few at Moon or Mars gravity, where astronauts are headed next. Our model agrees with all 133 BASS-II and Saffire burns we checked and estimates the gravity levels in between. Crews can’t evacuate a fire on a long mission, so designers need to catch risks before anything is built. Forman also shows where new NASA tests are most needed
details:
What it does and how it works

Forman is a website for planning Moon and Mars habitats with fire safety in mind. You lay out a base on a grid, or start from a photo, a sketch, a short description or a 3D model. Then you set the gravity (Earth, the ISS, the Moon, Mars or a custom value) and the cabin air. Forman checks every surface in every room and colors each room green, yellow or red depending on whether a fire there could keep burning, and the safety of the building.

You can also step inside a room in 3D, swap materials (cotton for Nomex, for example) and light a test fire to see how it would spread throughout the building. The flame changes shape with gravity: a teardrop on Earth, rounder on Mars and the Moon, almost a ball in orbit. A fire spread mode shows how fast a fire could move between rooms and whether the crew can still reach the airlock. If you ask for suggestions, the SI recommends fixes and highlights important tradeoffs and major changes to weight, oxygen percentage, and pressure, and our fire model re-checks every one before you can apply it.

The fire model is built from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data. Each material’s limit sits just under the lowest oxygen level NASA saw it keep burning at in microgravity, so it gets all 133 BASS-II and Saffire burns we checked it against right. NASA has no fire tests near the Moon or Mars gravity yet, so those values are estimated between the 0 g and 1 g results.

Benefits

NASA has run over 1,100 microgravity fire tests, but they’re spread across many experiments and hard to compare. Forman puts them in one place. It shows what was tested, what wasn’t, and what that means for a real habitat design, so engineers can catch fire risks before anything is built.

Intended impact

Safer Moon and Mars bases, and a clearer picture for NASA of which fire tests to run next. Almost none of NASA’s tests match Moon or Mars gravity or the oxygen-rich air planned for those bases. The same ideas apply on Earth wherever people live in sealed spaces, such as submarines, aircraft and mines.

Tools we used

  • Website: TypeScript and React, built with Vite.
  • 3D: three.js through React Three Fiber and drei.
  • Charts: visx.
  • Machine learning: Python with scikit-learn and NumPy, trained on 590 NASA runs. The trained models are exported so they run in the browser with no server.
  • SI features: Anthropic’s Claude (Sonnet and Haiku), called through Cloudflare Pages Functions so no API keys are in the browser.
  • Hosting and testing: Cloudflare Pages, with Vitest and pytest for tests and GitHub for teamwork.
  • Data: NASA’s PSI combustion database.
  • Hardware: just our laptops.

What makes it creative

Most fire data is shown as tables and charts. We turned it into rooms you can walk into and set on fire. Changing the gravity changes how the flame looks and behaves, so you can see the main idea of the challenge instead of just reading about it. The AI suggests fixes, but it never decides what’s safe: every verdict comes from a model tied to real NASA burns.

What we considered

  • Being honest about the data. Anything that’s our estimate is labeled. Moon and Mars values are marked as estimated, and we say clearly that this isn’t flight certification.
  • The real conditions for a Moon base: low gravity and NASA’s planned air of 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi.
  • Trade-offs. A safer material can add weight, and weight is expensive to send to the Moon, so suggestions show the added mass and cost.
  • Accessibility. Risk is always shown with color, an icon and a word, not color alone.
  • Who would use it. Students, researchers and habitat/fire hazard engineers.
  • Working offline. If the AI isn’t available, the rest of the site still works.
